newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK lauds handover party, but pressing issues lurk.
newsitem.headline: HK lauds handover party, but pressing issues lurk.

text.p: Hong Kong newspapers on Saturday lauded a breakthrough agreement between China and Britain on a joint ceremony for Hong Kong's handover next year, but newspapers and analysts said major transitional issues still need ironing out.

The countries signed an agreement on Friday to stage a spectacle of flag-changing and national anthems when London hands its last major colony back to Beijing at midnight on June 30, 1997, after more than 150 years of British rule.

The ceremony, envisaged by both parties to be grand and dignified, would be staged in the foyer of a convention centre along Hong Kong's famed Wanchai waterfront, with a capacity for over 4,000 people, including dignitaries all over the world.
The agreement also ended years of speculation in Hong Kong whether China and Britain, which had bickered for so long over handover details, would be able to agree on the joint ceremony.
Observers and newspaper commentators in the colony, however, received the news with measured applause.

"We should not forget the range of transitional issues, especially the selection of the Chief Executive," said Peter Cheung, assistant professor with the political science department at the University of Hong Kong.

With just 276 days to go before the handover, the territory is jittery over who would be its next leader and over Beijing's intention to dismantle its elected legislature and replace it with a provisional one.
Worries run high over the representativeness of a 400-member body, now being formed, which will choose the post-handover leader or Chief Executive, and form the provisional legislature.

Hong Kong democrats have called on London to challenge in court the legality of the provisional chamber, while independent legislator Christine Loh called on Beijing this week to invite the current elected legislators to serve beyond the handover to ensure a smooth transition.
The South China Morning Post said various transitional questions needed to be addressed urgently.

"Deep divisions remain, and there is no point in glossing over them. Indeed, they should be recognised and discussed in as great depth as possible in the coming nine months - not as intractable points of discord but for the benefit of Hong Kong's future way of life," a commentary in the newspaper said.
A China-backed Chinese-lanaguage daily Ta Kung Pao, however, urged London to continue cooperating with Beijing.

"The ceremony is but for a while. If the British side wants to end a historical chapter gloriously, it must cooperate with the Chinese side to work towards a successful and stable transition for Hong Kong," its commentary said.
